title: AI, China, and the New Risks to U.S. Security: Q&A with Matan Chorev
gist: Matan Chorev, who leads RAND Global and Emerging Risks, argues that rapid AI advancement will frustrate rather than enable states' pursuit of strategic autonomy, since even the U.S. and China will remain dependent on external chips, compute, capital, talent, and energy, while the power gap between great powers and emerging states widens.

insights.claim: A widely held post-Cold War assumption is that many states are moving toward strategic autonomy — more freedom of action, diverse relationships, fewer strategic dependencies, and more influence — but RAND research finds the rapid advance of AI is likely to frustrate that ambition.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers betting on a multipolar world of increasingly autonomous middle powers should reassess: AI dependency chains may instead re-concentrate leverage among a small set of resource-holders.
insights.quote: AI is likely to frustrate ambitions for strategic autonomy.
insights.locator: My colleague Salman Ahmed and I asked whether

insights.claim: Major powers including the United States and China will find it harder than expected to convert AI advantages into geopolitical dominance because they will still depend on external players for key resources, inputs, and markets.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Even AI-leading great powers face persistent supply-chain and market dependencies, implying continued value in the chokepoint suppliers (chips, energy, critical materials) rather than full self-sufficiency for either superpower.
insights.quote: Major powers like the United States and China will find it harder than they hoped to translate advantages in AI into geopolitical dominance.
insights.locator: Major powers like the United States and China

insights.claim: Emerging powers will see the capability gap with great powers grow rather than shrink because none of them holds the full combination of chips, compute, capital, talent, and energy needed to develop frontier AI.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Frontier-AI capability is likely to remain concentrated among a handful of resource-rich states, widening geopolitical and economic inequality rather than diffusing power as some multipolarity theses assume.
insights.quote: the gap between them and the great powers will grow, rather than shrink, since none of them possesses the combination of inputs—chips, compute, capital, talent, and energy—needed to develop frontier AI

insights.claim: These dynamics will require states of all sizes to rethink their national security and diplomatic strategies as the AI-driven redistribution of leverage unfolds.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Signals a coming wave of strategy revisions across foreign ministries and defense establishments, creating advisory and policy-research demand and shifting alliance calculations.
insights.quote: The implications of this will require states large and small to rethink their national security and diplomatic strategies.

themes.theme: RAND Global and Emerging Risks mission

insights.claim: RAND Global and Emerging Risks models its current mission on RAND's founding era after World War II, when the postwar order and the implications of nuclear weapons were still unclear and required foundational strategic analysis.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Frames the current AI moment as comparable in magnitude to the dawn of the nuclear era, suggesting demand for a new generation of strategy, doctrine, and capability-building institutions.
insights.locator: We take a lot of inspiration from RAND's

insights.claim: Chorev argues the assumptions that animated U.S. foreign policy and national security during the post-Cold War era no longer hold, and the nature of the emerging international order remains hazy.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: A senior RAND strategist publicly stating that post-Cold War policy assumptions are obsolete is a signal for investors to discount frameworks built on that era's stability assumptions.
insights.quote: The world as we knew it in the post–Cold War era no longer exists.
insights.locator: We're at a similar inflection point today

insights.claim: Unlike the nuclear era, governments do not control AI technology, and the trajectory and implications of AI are deeply uncertain, both of which make anticipatory government planning especially difficult.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Private-sector control of the core technology (versus state-controlled nuclear weapons) means corporate AI labs and chipmakers, not just governments, are now central actors in national-security planning — relevant for regulatory and public-private engagement strategy.
insights.locator: One is just that, unlike in the nuclear era

insights.claim: AI is not merely a national security capability but is touching labor markets, manufacturing, and the social and political foundations of democracy, making societal coordination — not just government policy — a key obstacle to preparedness.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: Broadens the AI-risk lens beyond defense/tech investing into labor markets and democratic institutions, implying spillover risk for sectors not traditionally viewed as national-security-adjacent.
insights.quote: AI is also not just a national security capability. It's touching every part of our lives—our labor market, our manufacturing, the social and political questions that are at the root of our democracy.
insights.locator: AI is also not just a national security

insights.claim: Chorev warns that transformative AI-driven change is coming, potentially very soon, and that failing to prepare for it risks catastrophic consequences for U.S. national security and for humanity broadly.
insights.speaker: Matan Chorev
insights.so_what: A high-conviction, near-term warning from a senior national-security strategist about catastrophic downside risk from unprepared AI transformation — relevant to tail-risk hedging and policy-timeline expectations.
insights.quote: Failing to prepare for these transformations is preparing to fail.
